Read the video transcript

Before you choose a car, choose who you want to help. Start with one customer situation, like a local driver whose car is being repaired. What do they need most? How could your rental help? Treat your answers as a starting idea, not proven demand. In the worksheet, describe your customer, their need, your offer, and one thing you will research next.

YOUR FLEET COACH

“Before you choose a car, choose who you want to help.”

Your first small win

Get specific about who you serve.

“Anyone who needs a car” is too broad for a useful first plan. Start with a customer situation you can investigate, then identify what a good rental would need to provide.

A sample customer profile

Local drivers whose own car is being repaired, looking for a temporary rental with clear pricing and a convenient pickup.

An illustration—not evidence of demand in your area.
Who needs the car?Name a customer and their situation.
What matters to them?Identify a practical need you can investigate.
See how to make an idea stronger

Too broad: People who want affordable cars.

More useful: Local drivers waiting on a repair who need a straightforward pickup and a clearly explained rental total.

This is a starting hypothesis. In Lesson 1.2, you would research whether your market supports it.

Watch or read, then complete your customer profile.

Do · One customer profile

Make it yours.

Short answers are enough. Use a business idea, not a real renter’s personal information.

Describe their situation, not just “everyone.”

Think about convenience, vehicle use, or clear communication.

Describe a service you could realistically deliver.

Pick one way to test your assumption.

I’m stuck. Give me a starting point.

Choose one situation: a visitor arriving in town, a local driver waiting on a repair, or a family needing a larger car for a trip. Treat it as an idea to research, not a proven business opportunity.
